blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind by division, and is written a to b. It has no unit, because the units cancel.

A proportion is a part divided by the whole it came from. It runs from zero to one, and a percentage is a proportion multiplied by one hundred.

A rate is a count divided by the quantity of something else it was counted over: time, or people, or both at once.

Two rates may be compared only when their denominators are the same.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Twelve grams against twenty grams is a ratio of twelve to twenty, or three to five.

If three of every five children in a room had the meal, the proportion is three fifths, or 0.6. A proportion can never be more than one.

Five kilograms a month is a rate. Fifteen deaths per thousand people per year is a rate.

The bottom of a rate is not a footnote. It is part of the number. Change it and you have a different quantity, even when the digits look the same.

blocks.label: Illustration
blocks.html:
Go back to section 3(1) of the National Food Security Act, 2013, which you opened two sections ago. It gives a person in a priority household five kilograms of foodgrains per person per month. This time read the sentence after it.

A proviso just below sets a different figure for households covered by the Antyodaya Anna Yojana. It is thirty-five kilograms of foodgrains per household per month. That figure applies to the extent the Central Government specifies for each State under that scheme.

Here is the sentence somebody writes.

Antyodaya households get seven times as much as priority households.

Look at where that seven came from. Thirty-five divided by five. The arithmetic is perfect and the claim is meaningless, because the five is per person and the thirty-five is per household. Two different denominators went into one division.

Make them the same and the picture changes. Take a household of six people.

5 kilograms per person per month, times 6 people
= 30 kilograms per household per month

35 against 30
35 minus 30 = 5 kilograms more
5 divided by 30 = 0.1666…, so about 17 per cent more

Seventeen per cent more, not seven times as much.

Now change the household and watch the answer move.

household of 7:    5 times 7 = 35, so the two are identical
household of 3:    5 times 3 = 15, so 35 is more than twice as much
household of 10: 5 times 10 = 50, so 35 is less

The comparison does not have one answer. It depends entirely on the denominator that the original sentence dropped.

One more thing to take from this, because it comes up in every table you will read. Rates for uncommon events are written per thousand or per hundred thousand people rather than per person. The only reason is to avoid a string of zeros after the point. Fifteen per thousand and 0.015 per person are the same rate.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
Making the denominators match is arithmetic. Deciding which denominator is the right one is not, and this section cannot help you with it.

So the conversion above is a tool for catching a false comparison. It is not a way of deciding who is better off.

And a rate per thousand people says nothing about which thousand. One figure for a state can hold districts that differ several times over. The rate will not show you that. It was never built to.

points.html: Two rates with different denominators cannot be compared, and dividing one by the other still produces a number.
Say the denominator out loud before you use any rate: per what, and over how long. If either half is missing you do not have a quantity yet.
Indian entitlements and scheme figures move between per person, per household and per beneficiary without warning. Read the whole provision, including the proviso, before you take a number out of it.
When two schemes are stated on different denominators, find the point at which they are equal and quote that.
Converting a per-household figure to a per-person one using an average household size assumes every household is average.
Asked to say which of two programmes delivers more, do not answer with the larger number. Ask what each is divided by.
Rates per thousand or per hundred thousand exist only to keep the zeros off the page. Convert freely, and check the denominator first whenever two tables disagree.

blocks.prompt: A block has 1,200 priority households with an average of five people each, and 300 Antyodaya households. Use section 3(1) of the National Food Security Act, 2013 and the proviso beneath it. Work out the monthly foodgrain entitlement of each group, and of the block as a whole. Then state the grain per household per month for each group and say which is higher.
blocks.answer:
Priority households first. They are entitled per person, so count the people.

1,200 households times 5 people = 6,000 people
6,000 people times 5 kilograms per person per month = 30,000 kilograms per month

Antyodaya households are entitled per household, so count the households.

300 households times 35 kilograms per household per month = 10,500 kilograms per month

The block as a whole.

30,000 plus 10,500 = 40,500 kilograms per month

Now put both on the same denominator, which is kilograms per household per month.

priority:    30,000 divided by 1,200 = 25
Antyodaya: 10,500 divided by 300    = 35

Antyodaya is higher on this denominator, at 35 against 25. Note what did the work: the average of five people a household. At an average of seven they would be equal, and above seven the priority households would come out ahead.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a line from a district presentation.

Grain offtake rose from 1,850 tonnes to 2,050 tonnes, so coverage improved by 11 per cent.

The arithmetic in the percentage is right. Name the step that is missing, and say what you would ask for.
blocks.answer:
The percentage is a rate of change in tonnes. It is being reported as a change in coverage, which is a proportion of people. Those are different quantities and nothing in the line connects them.

Tonnes can rise for at least three reasons that have nothing to do with more people being covered.

  • More households on the list.
  • The same households lifting a larger share of what they were already entitled to.
  • A change in what the entitlement is.

What to ask for, in this order. How many people or households were entitled in each period, so the tonnes have a denominator. How much they were entitled to in total. Then the offtake can be read as a proportion of the entitlement rather than as a bare weight. Only then does the word coverage have anything underneath it.

And keep the 11 per cent. It is a perfectly good statement about tonnes. It has simply been given the wrong noun.

blocks.prompt:
Reduce each ratio as far as it will go.

18 to 24    45 to 15    200 to 500
blocks.answer:
18 to 24    = 3 to 4    (divide both by 6)
45 to 15    = 3 to 1    (divide both by 15)
200 to 500 = 2 to 5    (divide both by 100)

A ratio reduces the way a fraction does. It is a division written another way.

None of the three carries a unit. Whatever the 18 and the 24 were measured in has cancelled out, and that is what makes a ratio a bare number.

blocks.prompt: Of 250 households in a block, 90 lift their full entitlement. Write that as a ratio of lifting to not lifting, and as a proportion of all households.
blocks.answer:
The ratio first. Lifting against not lifting means 90 against the rest.

250 minus 90 = 160 not lifting
90 to 160 = 9 to 16    (divide both by 10)

Now the proportion, which is out of all of them.

90 divided by 250 = 0.36

Nine to sixteen, and 0.36.

Notice the two denominators. The ratio is against the 160 who did not; the proportion is against all 250. Neither number is wrong and they answer different questions.

blocks.prompt: A rate is 15 per 1,000 people per year. Write the same rate per 100,000 people per year, and per person per year.
blocks.answer:
Per 100,000 first. That is a hundred times as many people, so a hundred times as many events.

15 times 100 = 1,500 per 100,000 per year

Per person, divide by a thousand.

15 divided by 1,000 = 0.015 per person per year

One rate, three ways of writing it. Nothing has been measured differently, and none of the three is more precise than the others. The denominator was chosen to keep the zeros off the page.

blocks.prompt: Section 3(1) of the National Food Security Act, 2013 gives 5 kilograms per person per month. A household of four is entitled under it. Work out the household’s entitlement per month and per year, and state the denominator of each answer.
blocks.answer:
5 kilograms per person per month, times 4 people
= 20 kilograms per household per month
20 times 12 months
= 240 kilograms per household per year

The denominators, said out loud. The first is per household per month. The second is per household per year.

Both had to change together when you multiplied by four: the per-person denominator became a per-household one, and that is the step worth watching. The number 20 means nothing until it carries “per household per month” with it.

blocks.prompt: Under the proviso to section 3(1), an Antyodaya household gets 35 kilograms per household per month. Work out the household size at which a priority household on 5 kilograms per person per month receives the same amount.
blocks.answer:
Put both on the same denominator, which is kilograms per household per month.

priority household of n people = 5 times n
set that equal to 35
5 times n = 35
n = 35 divided by 5
n = 7

Seven people.

That number is worth carrying. Below seven, an Antyodaya household receives more; above seven, a priority household does. “They match at a household of seven” is a sentence that settles an argument, and it took one division.

blocks.prompt: A block has 3,200 people and records 48 events in a year. A second block has 12,500 people and records 160 events in a year. Work out each rate per 1,000 people per year and say which is higher.
blocks.answer:
First block.

48 divided by 3,200 = 0.015 per person per year
times 1,000 = 15 per 1,000 per year

Second block.

160 divided by 12,500 = 0.0128 per person per year
times 1,000 = 12.8 per 1,000 per year

The first block is higher, at 15 against 12.8, even though it recorded fewer events.

That reversal is the point of the problem. The raw counts say 48 against 160. The rates say the opposite, because the second block has nearly four times the people.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

in a block, 72 households lift their full entitlement and 108 do not
the ratio of lifting to not lifting is 72 to 108, or 2 to 3
72 divided by 108 = 0.6666…
so about 67 per cent of households lift their full entitlement
blocks.answer:
The first two lines hold. Seventy-two against 108 is the ratio, and it does reduce to 2 to 3.

The step that broke is the last one. A ratio has been divided out and the answer read as a proportion. A ratio compares one part with another part. A proportion is a part over the whole it came from, and the whole here is every household in the block.

72 plus 108 = 180 households in all
72 divided by 180 = 0.4
times 100 = 40 per cent lift their full entitlement

Forty per cent, not 67.

The 0.6666 is not a meaningless number. It says the lifting households are two thirds as many as the households that do not lift. That is true. It has been given the wrong denominator and then the wrong noun.

Why it looks reasonable: a ratio and a proportion are both one number divided by another, and both come out as a decimal. A decimal below one invites being read as a percentage. The check is to say the denominator out loud. Divided by 108 is per non-lifting household. Divided by 180 is per household.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

block A: 15 cases per 1,000 people
block B: 40 cases per 100,000 people
40 is more than 15, so block B is worse
blocks.answer:
The step that broke is the comparison, which sets two rates side by side without matching their denominators.

Put both on the same denominator.

block A: 15 per 1,000
= 15 times 100
= 1,500 per 100,000
block B: 40 per 100,000

Block A is nearly forty times block B, not the other way round.

Why it looks reasonable: both lines end in “people”, both numbers are small, and the larger number belongs to the block being called worse. Everything about the shape of the sentence is right except the only thing that mattered.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

a scheme delivers 2 kg per person per week
a month is 4 weeks
so it delivers 8 kg per person per month
a household has 5 people
so it delivers 8 kg per household per month
blocks.answer:
The first three lines hold. Two kilograms a week for four weeks is eight kilograms a month.

The step that broke is the last one. The denominator was changed from per person to per household with no arithmetic done at all.

8 kilograms per person per month, times 5 people
= 40 kilograms per household per month

Forty, not eight.

Why it looks reasonable: the household size appears in the line just above, so the reader feels it has been used. It has been mentioned. Mentioning a denominator is not the same as dividing or multiplying by it.

blocks.prompt:
A note crosses your desk with one line in it.

Households here average five people, so an Antyodaya household gets 40 per cent more grain.

Section 3(1) of the National Food Security Act, 2013 gives 5 kilograms per person per month. The proviso beneath it gives an Antyodaya household 35 kilograms per household per month. Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: both entitlements on one denominator, which is kilograms per household per month.

priority household of 5: 5 times 5 = 25 kilograms per household per month
Antyodaya household:    35 kilograms per household per month
35 minus 25 = 10
10 divided by 25 = 0.4, so 40 per cent more

The 40 per cent is right, for a household of five.

Now the part the line hides. It is a statement about the average household, and the average household is a calculation rather than an address. Run the same division at other sizes.

household of 3: 5 times 3 = 15, so 35 is well over twice as much
household of 7: 5 times 7 = 35, so the two are equal
household of 9: 5 times 9 = 45, so the priority household gets more

The gap is 40 per cent at one household size, nothing at all at another, and the other way round above seven.

What this does not establish. It says nothing about how household sizes are spread here. An average of five holds whether every household has five people or half have two and half have eight. It says nothing about how many households are in either group. And it says nothing about whether either figure feeds anybody, which is a different question from which is larger.

blocks.prompt:
A journalist calls with one line and wants a comment by the evening.

District A has twice the case rate of district B, so it needs twice the resources.

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
Nothing can be computed until one thing is known: what each rate is divided by.

Suppose both are per 1,000 people, and A has 2 lakh people and B has 8 lakh. Then a doubled rate is not a doubled count.

district A: 20 per 1,000, times 200 thousand people = 4,000 cases
district B: 10 per 1,000, times 800 thousand people = 8,000 cases

Twice the rate and half the cases. Resources follow people, so the conclusion is backwards.

Those population figures are made up, to show the move. The move is not. Ask for the two denominators before you agree or disagree with the sentence.

What this does not establish. Even with both counts in hand, nothing here says what resource a case needs, or whether the two districts counted cases the same way. A rate comparison decides which question to ask next, not what to do.
